Testifieth
tĕs'tĭ-fī-eth
v. (third person singular of testify: to bear witness, to affirm as an eyewitness; rendering Greek martureo)
Latin testificari, from testis, a witness. The Greek martureo gives English martyr: the witness who seals his testimony with his blood.

Biblical Definition

The word runs from indictment to benediction. Hosea: “the pride of Israel testifieth to his face” (Hos 7:10) — a man's own pride is a witness against him in court, and needs no other accuser. John the Baptist of Christ: “what he hath seen and heard, that he testifieth; and no man receiveth his testimony” (Joh 3:32) — the perfect Witness, reporting the Father's house from firsthand sight, and the world declining the evidence. John of himself at the close of the Gospel: “This is the disciple which testifieth of these things, and wrote these things: and we know that his testimony is true” (Joh 21:24) — the apostolic claim to eyewitness authority on which the canon rests. The writer to the Hebrews of the Son's priesthood: “For he testifieth, Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec” (Heb 7:17), where the Scripture itself is the one testifying. And at the end of the Book: “He which testifieth these things saith, Surely I come quickly” (Rev 22:20). Christianity is not a philosophy deduced; it is a testimony borne. That is why its central verb is a courtroom verb, and why its witnesses were prepared to die rather than amend the record.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to testify as to make a solemn declaration, verbal or written, to establish a fact; to bear witness; to affirm or declare solemnly.

expand to see more

TESTIFY, v.i. To make a solemn declaration, verbal or written, to establish some fact; to give testimony for the purpose of communicating to others a knowledge of something not known to them.

2. In Scripture, to affirm or declare solemnly.

TESTIFY, v.t. To bear witness to; to support the truth of by testimony; to affirm or declare.

Key Scripture

Joh 3:32 — "And what he hath seen and heard, that he testifieth; and no man receiveth his testimony."

Joh 21:24 — "This is the disciple which testifieth of these things, and wrote these things: and we know that his testimony is true."

Rev 22:20 — "He which testifieth these things saith, Surely I come quickly. Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus."

Modern Corruption

Testimony has been reduced to a report of private feeling, so that what a Christian testifies to is his own inner experience rather than a public fact he has seen.

expand to see more

John 21:24 is the seal on a book: this is the disciple which testifieth of these things, and wrote these things: and we know that his testimony is true. The claim is evidentiary. A man saw the risen Christ, ate broiled fish with Him by the sea of Tiberias, and wrote it down, and the church certifies the witness. That is what the New Testament means by testimony — the same word a Roman court would use, and the same standard: what a witness saw and heard. The modern church has largely reassigned the word to the interior life. A testimony has come to mean the story of how one came to feel about God as one now feels, which is not nothing but is not what martureo means and cannot bear the weight the New Testament puts on it. The two are easily distinguished by a question: if the witness is mistaken about his own feelings, someone is disappointed; if he is mistaken about the empty tomb, the whole faith is vain and we are found false witnesses of God. Paul says exactly that in 1 Corinthians 15. Christian testimony stakes itself on facts outside the witness, which is precisely why it was worth dying for.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek martureo (G3140), to bear witness, to testify; marturia (G3141), the testimony borne; martus (G3144), a witness, and so a martyr.

expand to see more

Greek martureo (G3140) — to bear witness, to affirm what one has seen and heard; John 3:32, 21:24, Revelation 22:20.

Greek marturia (G3141) — the testimony itself; the Spirit, the water, and the blood bear witness, and the witness of God is greater than that of men; 1 John 5:9.

Greek martus (G3144) — a witness; Stephen is called the Lord's martus and the word passed into English as martyr; Acts 22:20, Hebrews 12:1.

Usage

"“What he hath seen and heard, that he testifieth” — the perfect Witness reporting the Father."

"“We know that his testimony is true” — the church's certificate on the eyewitness."

"“He which testifieth these things saith, Surely I come quickly” — the last testimony in the canon."
